newsitem.title: UK: Company describes possible new diabetes drug.
newsitem.headline: Company describes possible new diabetes drug.

text.p: U.S. researchers said on Wednesday they had identified a possible new route for treating diabetes, using the complex interactions between cells.

Richard Heyman of Ligand Pharmaceuticals Inc in San Diego and colleagues at the University of Texas homed in on the retinoid X receptor (RXR), a cell receptor that acts as a partner to other cell receptors involved in hormone signalling.

Drugs that stimulate RXR counteract the effects of non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM or type II diabetes), including the high blood sugar, insulin and blood fat levels, at least in genetically engineered mice, they wrote in a report in the science journal Nature.

Hayman's group used "ob" and "db" mice, whose genes have been altered to make them resemble obese and diabetic humans. They dosed them with drugs known as ligands, which bind, or attach, to certain cell receptors.
The ligands in this case were LG100268 and LGD1069, which bind specifically to RXR. Ligand Pharmaceuticals is developing and testing LGD1069 as Targretin.
They worked nearly as well as another drug, thiazolidinedione (TZD), recently approved for use in diabetes, and even better when used along with it, they wrote.
"These studies demonstrate that RXR agonists function as insulin sensitizers, markedly decreasing serum glucose, triglycerides and insulin," Heyman's group wrote.

"It is appropriate that RXR activators be considered a distinct class of pharmacological agents and could be referred to as 'rexinoids' to distinguish their activity from retinoids' (used to describe vitamin A derivatives)," they suggested.
Ligand Pharmaceuticals announced last week it was starting Phase II clinical trials of Targretin in diabetic patients in Belgium and Netherlands.
It is also testing Targretin against cancer.

RXRs play an important role in programmed cell death or "apoptosis," which is when damaged cells destroy themselves. A failure of apoptosis can lead to the uncontrolled cell division that marks cancer. -- Maggie Fox, London Newsroom 44-171-542-8958
